claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and comparison with phiX.

claims.claim: Gokushoviruses lack a major spike protein involved in host cell attachment.
claims.source: (ii) a major spike protein involved in host cell attachment (Doore and Fane, 2016; Roux et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on gokushovirus and phiX genomics.

claims.claim: The absence of peptidoglycan synthesis inhibitor and major spike protein from gokushoviruses indicates that these phages might operate quite differently from phiX on a molecular level.
claims.source: These proteins represent crucial elements in the infectious cycle of phiX, and their absence from other gokushoviruses indicates that these phages might operate quite differently on a molecular level.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic differences between gokushoviruses and phiX.

claims.claim: A large number of gokushovirus prophages are integrated into the genomes of enterobacteria.
claims.source: Here we detect a large number of gokushovirus prophages integrated into the genomes of enterobacteria, contrasting with their predicted exclusively lytic lifestyle.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the bioinformatic analysis presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: Through transformation of a synthesized prophage genome into a laboratory strain of Escherichia coli, a novel gokushovirus capable of lysogenizing enterobacteria was cultivated.
claims.source: Through transformation of a synthesized prophage genome into a laboratory strain of Escherichia coli, we cultivate a novel gokushovirus capable of lysogenizing enterobacteria.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the experimental work described in the Results section.

claims.claim: The gokushovirus EC6098 is capable of passive integration via XerC/XerD mediated recombination of phage encoded dif-motifs with their bacterial counterparts.
claims.source: Using this experimental model system, we demonstrate that this phage is capable of passive integration via XerC/XerD mediated recombination of phage encoded dif-motifs with their bacterial counterparts.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic complementation and mutant analysis experiments.

claims.claim: The capability for XerC/XerD-mediated integration has evolved independently in multiple lineages of gokushoviruses.
claims.source: We also show that this capability has evolved independently in multiple lineages of gokushoviruses
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of dif-motifs across gokushovirus lineages.

claims.claim: There exists an intermediate, pseudolysogenic step between lytic and lysogenic lifestyle in gokushoviruses.
claims.source: and demonstrate the existence of an intermediate, pseudolysogenic step between lytic and lysogenic lifestyle
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through serial transfer experiments with phages lacking complete integration machinery.

claims.claim: Gokushoviruses can lead a decidedly different existence from that of previously characterized members of the Gokushovirinae.
claims.source: indicating that gokushoviruses can lead a decidedly different existence from that of previously characterized members of the Gokushovirinae.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing lysogenic and pseudolysogenic capabilities.

claims.claim: Querying fully assembled bacterial genomes with the major capsid protein VP1 of gokushovirus Chlamydia-phage 4 returned 95 high-confidence hits within the Enterobacteriaceae.
claims.source: Querying fully assembled bacterial genomes with the major capsid protein VP1 of gokushovirus Chlamydia-phage 4 (NCBI Gene ID 3703676) returned 95 high-confidence hits (E-value <0.0001) within the Enterobacteriaceae (91 from Escherichia, and one each from Enterobacter, Salmonella, Citrobacter and Kosakonia; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct result from the bioinformatic analysis performed in the study.

claims.claim: Inspection of genomic regions revealed the presence of integrated prophages 4300–4700 bp in length with a conserved six-gene arrangement: VP4, VP5, VP3, VP1, VP2 and VP8.
claims.source: Although Gokushovirinae were previously known only as lytic phages, inspection of each of the associated genomic regions revealed the presence of integrated prophages 4300–4700 bp in length and having a conserved six-gene arrangement: VP4 (replication initiation protein), VP5 (switch from dsDNA to ssDNA replication protein), VP3 (scaffold protein), VP1 (major capsid protein), VP2 (minor capsid protein) and VP8 (putative DNA-binding protein).
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the detected prophages.

claims.claim: Most of the variation in genome size and sequence of enterogokushovirus prophages is confined to three regions: near the C-terminus of VP2, in the non-coding region between VP8 and VP2, and within VP1.
claims.source: Most of the variation in both the genome size and sequence of these prophages is confined to three regions: (i) near the C-terminus of VP2, (ii) in the non-coding region between VP8 and VP2, and (iii) within VP1, whose hypervariability is characteristic of the Gokushovirinae (Chipman et al., 1998; Diemer and Stedman, 2016; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and analysis, with reference to Figure 1A and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: All detected prophages are flanked by dif-motifs, which are 28 bp palindromic sites that are known to be the targets of passive integration by phages and other mobile elements.
claims.source: All detected prophages are flanked by dif-motifs, which are 28 bp palindromic sites that are known to be the targets of passive integration by phages and other mobile elements (Blakely et al., 1993; Das et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citations to previous work on dif-motifs.

claims.claim: The dif-motifs upstream of the insertions are highly conserved and individually differ by, at most, one nucleotide from the canonical dif-motif of Escherichia coli.
claims.source: The dif-motifs upstream of the insertions are highly conserved and individually differ by, at most, one nucleotide from the canonical dif-motif of Escherichia coli.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and comparison of the detected dif-motifs.

claims.claim: The upstream dif-motifs consist of a central 6 bp spacer flanked by two 11 bp arms, which bind tyrosine recombinases XerC/XerD during chromosome segregation and integration of mobile elements.
claims.source: These upstream dif-motifs consist of a central 6 bp spacer flanked by two 11 bp arms, previously been shown to bind tyrosine recombinases XerC/XerD during chromosome segregation and integration of mobile elements (Castillo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by a citation to previous work on XerC/XerD binding.

claims.claim: The dif-motifs downstream of detected prophages are more variable, particularly in the spacer region and XerD-binding arms, representing the phage dif-motifs integrated along with the phage.
claims.source: In contrast, the dif-motifs downstream of detected prophages are more variable, particularly in the spacer region and XerD-binding arms, representing the phage dif-motifs integrated along with the phage (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: A whole genome phylogeny of gokushovirus prophages shows a number of well-differentiated lineages, forming clades A-J that each contains members with >95% average nucleotide identity, and 14 singleton lineages with no close relatives.
claims.source: A whole genome phylogeny of gokushovirus prophages shows a number of well-differentiated (bootstrap support 70% or higher) lineages, forming clades A-J that each contains members with >95% average nucleotide identity, and 14 singleton lineages with no close relatives (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Prophages belonging to clade A-D are found dispersed across the host phylogeny, while prophage clade I is confined to a single E. coli clade.
claims.source: For example, whereas prophages belonging to clade A-D are found dispersed across the host phylogeny, prophage clade I is confined to a single E. coli clade (possibly as a result of the limited number of detected prophages).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of phage and host phylogenies shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In all but one case, each E. coli host harbors only a single gokushovirus prophage.
claims.source: In all but one case, each E. coli host harbors only a single gokushovirus prophage.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the detected prophages in bacterial genomes.

claims.claim: There is no obvious association between the presence of gokushovirus prophages and particular E. coli O-serotypes among those strains for which information on O-antigens is available.
claims.source: Although phage attachment and infection sometimes depend on O-antigenicity, there is no obvious association between the presence of gokushovirus prophages and particular E. coli O-serotypes among those strains for which information on O-antigens is available (Zhou et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of O-serotype data for strains harboring prophages.

claims.claim: Four identical prophages belonging to clade C were detected in E. coli strains MOD1-EC5200 (O76:H19), MOD1-EC5181 (O132:H8), NCTC9043 (O43:H2) and MOD1-EC6266 (O124:H21).
claims.source: For example, four identical prophages belonging to clade C could be detected in E. coli strains MOD1-EC5200 (O76:H19), MOD1-EC5181 (O132:H8), NCTC9043 (O43:H2) and MOD1-EC6266 (O124:H21) (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and O-serotype data.

claims.claim: Most gokushovirus prophages were detected in diverse E. coli strains isolated from various animals, mainly cattle and marmots.
claims.source: Most gokushovirus prophages were detected in diverse E. coli strains isolated from various animals, mainly cattle and marmots, but five prophages were detected in isolates from humans, including one from a urinary tract infection (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on metadata associated with the bacterial strains harboring prophages.

claims.claim: Five prophages were detected in isolates from humans, including one from a urinary tract infection.
claims.source: but five prophages were detected in isolates from humans, including one from a urinary tract infection (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on metadata associated with the bacterial strains harboring prophages.

claims.claim: Enterobacterial prophages form a well-supported, monophyletic clade within the Gokushovirinae.
claims.source: Phylogenetic analysis of available gokushovirus genomes based on an alignment of the conserved VP1 and VP4 proteins (n = 855; including the enterobacterial prophages discovered in this study, the previously sequenced lytic gokushoviruses from Chlamydia, Spiroplasma and Bdellovibrio, and the metagenomically assembled gokushovirus genomes available from NCBI) returned enterobacterial prophages as a well-supported (97% bootstrap support), monophyletic clade within the Gokushovirinae (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The distinctiveness of the enterobacterial prophage clade, whose members share a conserved gene order and display an average nucleotide identity of >50%, advocates the formation of a new proposed genus within the family Microviridae (subfamily Gokushovirinae), named Enterogokushovirus.
claims.source: The distinctiveness of this clade, whose members share a conserved (but not unique) gene order and display an average nucleotide identity of >50% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2), advocates the formation of a new proposed genus within the family Microviridae (subfamily Gokushovirinae), for which we suggest the name Enterogokushovirus on account of a distribution limited to members of the Enterobactericeae.
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and genomic analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A unique feature of enterogokushoviruses among the Gokushovirinae appears to be the ability to exist as lysogens.
claims.source: Since a unique feature of enterogokushoviruses among the Gokushovirinae appears to be the ability to exist as lysogens, we searched all other gokushovirus MAGs in our dataset for dif-like sequence motifs that might be indicative of lysogenic ability.
claims.evidence: This is based on the detection of integrated prophages and comparison with other gokushoviruses.

claims.claim: Similar dif-like motifs were detected in 48 genomes distributed sporadically throughout the gokushovirus phylogeny.
claims.source: We detected similar motifs in 48 genomes distributed sporadically throughout the gokushovirus phylogeny.
claims.evidence: This is based on bioinformatic search for dif-motifs in gokushovirus MAGs.

claims.claim: Aside from the enterogokushoviruses, there are two larger clades in which multiple genomes contain a dif-motif, with the rest of dif-bearing MAGs found largely as singletons.
claims.source: Aside from the enterogokushoviruses, there are two larger clades in which multiple genomes contain a dif-motif, with the rest of dif-bearing MAGs found largely as singletons (Figure 2; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and dif-motif detection, shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The majority of putative dif-motifs occurs in non-coding regions, and those detected within coding regions were typically at the 5'- or 3'-end of a predicted gene.
claims.source: The majority of these putative dif-motifs occurs in non-coding regions, and those detected within coding regions were typically at the 5'- or 3'-end of a predicted gene, with a nearby alternative start or stop codon that could preserve the genetic integrity of the phage through integration and excision.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the genomic context of detected dif-motifs.

claims.claim: The overall dearth of dif-like sequences in gokushoviruses sampled from diverse geographic and ecological settings highlights the distinctiveness of Enterogokushovirus genomes and lifestyle.
claims.source: The overall dearth of dif-like sequences in gokushoviruses sampled from diverse geographic and ecological settings highlights the distinctiveness of Enterogokushovirus genomes and lifestyle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative analysis of dif-motif distribution.

claims.claim: Only two integrated prophages corresponding to E. coli gokushoviruses were fully assembled from 1839 samples from eight metagenomic studies of human and cattle gut microbiomes.
claims.source: We further attempted to determine the prevalence of enterobacterial gokushoviruses by interrogating 1839 samples from eight metagenomic studies of human and cattle gut microbiomes for the presence of closely related prophages. From these data, we were able to fully assemble only two integrated prophages corresponding to E. coli gokushoviruses, one from the fecal metagenome of an Austrian adult (0,05% of all reads in ERR688616) and the other from a Danish infant (0,02% of all reads in ERR525761) (see also Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on metagenomic assembly from multiple datasets.

claims.claim: The integrity of prophage structure in all enterobacteria and the lack of premature stop codons suggested that these sequences represent intact, functional insertions into bacterial hosts.
claims.source: The integrity of prophage structure in all enterobacteria and the lack of premature stop codons suggested that these sequences represent intact, functional insertions into bacterial hosts.
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the detected prophages.

claims.claim: Sequences corresponding to prophages from four Escherichia strains were amplified, circularized and transformed into E. coli DH5α.
claims.source: To confirm the functionality of Escherichia gokushovirus prophages, characterize their biology and provide a type strain, we attempted to construct phages from genomic DNA of Escherichia strains MOD1-EC2703, MOD1-EC5150, MOD1-EC6098 and MOD1-EC6163, selected to represent the diversity of gokushovirus prophages and hosts (Figure 1B). Sequences corresponding to prophages from these four Escherichia strains were amplified, circularized and transformed into E. coli DH5α (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure performed, shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Supernatants from the transformed DH5α culture resulted in plaques for only one of four reconstructed phage genomes (EC6098) when used in agar-overlay assays with E. coli K12 BW25113 hosts.
claims.source: Supernatants from the transformed DH5α culture were used in agar-overlay assays with E. coli K12 BW25113 hosts, resulting in plaques for only one of four reconstructed phage genomes (EC6098, derived from E. marmotae strain MOD1-EC6098 and belonging to prophage clade E (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct experimental result shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: DH5α alone did not produce plaques on BW25113 and vice versa.
claims.source: While both DH5α and BW25113 possess other prophages which could produce false positives when screening for gokushovirus production (Chen et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2010), DH5α alone did not produce plaques on BW25113 and vice versa (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Circularized gokushovirus genomes were detected in all four strains (MOD1-EC2703, MOD1-EC5150, MOD1-EC6098 and MOD1-EC6163) via PCR, but only MOD1-EC6098 produced plaques.
claims.source: To corroborate the synthesis of EC6098 phages (and the inability to produce phages from the other three sequences), we additionally grew live cultures of MOD1-EC2703, MOD1-EC5150, MOD1-EC6098 and MOD1-EC6163 and via PCR detected the presence of circularized gokushovirus genomes in all four, but only MOD1-EC6098 produced plaques resembling those derived from synthetic EC6098 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Electron microscopic observation of pure EC6098 lysates revealed tailless icosahedral virions, 25–30 µm in size and displaying protrusions previously observed in other Gokushovirinae.
claims.source: Electron microscopic observation of pure EC6098 lysates recovered at a buoyant density of around 1.3 g/cm−3 in CsCl gradients (the range expected for members of the Microviridae, Thurber et al., 2009), revealed tailless icosahedral virions, 25–30 µm in size and displaying protrusions previously observed in other Gokushovirinae (Chipman et al., 1998; Diemer and Stedman, 2016; Figure 3D,E).
claims.evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D,E and supported by citations.

claims.claim: EC6098 represents the first isolation of a gokushovirus able to infect free-living bacteria as well as being able to integrate as a lysogen into bacterial genomes.
claims.source: Because Gokushovirinae have only been recovered as lytic particles from intracellular bacteria, this represents the first isolation of a gokushovirus able to infect free-living bacteria as well as being able to integrate as a lysogen into bacterial genomes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and comparison with previously known gokushoviruses.

claims.claim: The presence of circularized phage genomes could readily be detected from surviving colonies in confluent plaques derived from agar-overlay assays.
claims.source: We next investigated the process by which gokushoviruses integrate into the bacterial host chromosome (Figure 4A). The presence of circularized phage genomes could readily be detected from surviving colonies in confluent plaques derived from agar-overlay assays (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Using primers that flank both sides of the dif-motif in host strain BW25113, products were recovered that were enlarged by the length of the phage relative to colonies lacking the prophage.
claims.source: Using primers that flank both sides of the dif-motif in host strain BW25113, we recovered products that were enlarged by the length of the phage relative to colonies lacking the prophage (Figure 4A,C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4A,C.

claims.claim: Sequencing confirmed that phage EC6098 integrates downstream of the BW25113 dif-motif, which remains unchanged.
claims.source: Sequencing confirmed that, in accordance with the integration site of detected prophages, phage EC6098 integrates downstream of the BW25113 dif-motif, which remains unchanged (corresponding to position 3,046,436–3,046,463 in the closed genome with accession number CP009273).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequencing data confirming the integration site.

claims.claim: Neither ΔxerC nor ΔxerD mutants of E. coli host strain BW25113 resulted in integration.
claims.source: Because none of the gokushovirus prophages encodes an integrase, we predicted that host factors XerC and XerD might be responsible for prophage integration, similar to what has been hypothesized for microvirus-prophages in Bacteroidetes (Krupovic and Forterre, 2011). Neither ΔxerC nor ΔxerD mutants of E. coli host strain BW25113 resulted in integration
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result from infection assays with knockout mutants.

claims.claim: The ΔxerC mutant was restored by complementation with a plasmid expressing the intact version of xerC.
claims.source: but the ΔxerC mutant was restored by complementation with a plasmid expressing the intact version of xerC.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result from complementation assays.

claims.claim: Phages with incomplete or no dif-motifs successfully infected hosts but failed to integrate into host genomes.
claims.source: Similarly, phages with incomplete (i.e., lacking either their XerC or XerD binding site within the dif-motif, termed here ΔdifC and ΔdifD) or no dif-motifs (ΔdifCD) successfully infected hosts (as evidenced by the presence of circularized phage genomes in host colonies that had survived infection), but failed to integrate into host genomes, demonstrating the need for cooperative XerC/XerD binding for successful lysogeny (Table 1, Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Table 1, Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: The retention of dif-motifs after integration indicates that the integration process is reversible.
claims.source: However, the retention of dif-motifs after integration indicates that this process is reversible
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic structure of integrated prophages.

claims.claim: There is a smaller fragment in addition to that indicating prophage insertion, corresponding to those cells in the same colony that do not harbor the integrated prophage.
claims.source: As evident in Figure 4C, there is a smaller fragment, in addition to that indicating prophage insertion, that corresponds to those cells in the same colony that do not harbor the integrated prophage.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: These cells persisted even after multiple rounds of re-streaking, and the median ratio of lysogens to non-lysogenic cells derived from clonal colonies approaches 4:1.
claims.source: These cells persisted even after multiple rounds of re-streaking, and the median ratio of lysogens to non-lysogenic cells derived from clonal colonies approaches 4:1 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Even in pure cultures, phages are continuously being excised and reintegrated, presumably as a result of XerC/XerD activity.
claims.source: Even in pure cultures, phages are thus continuously being excised and reintegrated, presumably as a result of XerC/XerD activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of mixed lysogenic/non-lysogenic populations.

claims.claim: Almost all bacterial colonies that survived infections, regardless of whether they were lysogenized or not, were found to contain circular phage DNA.
claims.source: The removal of host factors xerC or xerD, the presence an incomplete phage dif-motif, or the lack of a dif-motif (as observed in the majority of Gokushovirinae) all prevent integration of phages into host genomes (Table 1, Figure 4C). However, almost all bacterial colonies that survived infections, regardless of whether they were lysogenized or not, were found to contain circular phage DNA (Figure 4B)
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The presence of circular phage DNA alone, regardless of integration into the host genome, conferred superinfection immunity.
claims.source: and the presence of circular phage DNA alone, regardless of integration into the host genome, conferred superinfection immunity (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Cultures in which phage DNA could only be detected in circularized form were capable of producing infectious particles at levels significantly higher than those of cultures containing integrated prophages.
claims.source: In addition, cultures in which phage DNA could only be detected in circularized form were capable of producing infectious particles at levels significantly higher than those of cultures containing integrated prophages (Figure 5B, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The absence of alternative integration sites was verified by inverse PCR.
claims.source: The absence of alternative integration sites, as verified by inverse PCR, suggested that gokushoviruses might be able to persist in the host cytoplasm without integration into the host genome.
claims.evidence: This is based on inverse PCR experiments.

claims.claim: Gokushoviruses might be able to persist in the host cytoplasm without integration into the host genome.
claims.source: The absence of alternative integration sites, as verified by inverse PCR, suggested that gokushoviruses might be able to persist in the host cytoplasm without integration into the host genome.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: All lysogenic cultures produced phage particles throughout the course of serial transfer experiments.
claims.source: To determine whether this persistence is a transient phenomenon that eventually leads to either the loss of phages or the collapse of bacterial cultures, we performed serial transfers (1:1000 dilution) with a variety of host-phage combinations over the course of a month. We enumerated plaque formation from culture supernatant on host strain BW25113ΔfhuA to avoid false positives from widespread contaminating dsDNA phages such as phi80 and SW-1, which unlike EC6098 require outer membrane receptor FhuA for successful infection (Rotman et al., 2012; Song et al., 2019). As expected, all lysogenic cultures (i.e., wild type cultures with integrated gokushovirus prophages) produced phage particles throughout the course of the experiments.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result from serial transfer experiments.

claims.claim: A third of all cultures where gokushoviruses were initially present only in the cytoplasm retained phage production over the course of a month despite the lack of integration.
claims.source: However, a third of all cultures where gokushoviruses were initially present only in the cytoplasm (due to deletions in the host integration machinery or phage integration site) retained phage production over the course of a month despite the lack of integration (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Gokushoviruses do not exist solely as lytic particles but can also exist as (pseudo)lysogens, in a carrier state that continuously produces phage particles without integrating into the genome.
claims.source: Cumulatively, these results indicate that gokushoviruses do not exist solely as lytic particles, as previously believed, but can also exist as (pseudo)lysogens, in a carrier state that continuously produces phage particles without integrating into the genome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results from serial transfer and integration experiments.

claims.claim: The new proposed genus, Enterogokushovirus, offers new insights into the understanding of the ecologically widespread group of Gokushovirinae phages.
claims.source: Through the analysis of whole genome sequences and metagenomic databases, we defined a unique genus of Gokushovirinae prophages and subsequently synthesized a viable gokushovirus capable of infecting and integrating into the genomes of enteric bacteria. Since Gokushovirinae were previously known as exclusively lytic predators of a few intracellular bacteria (King et al., 2011), the new proposed genus, Enterogokushovirus, offers new insights into our understanding of this ecologically widespread group of phages.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: By confirming the existence of Gokushovirinae prophages in free-living bacteria, a seeming paradox was resolved in which a diverse and widespread lineage within the Microviridae appeared to be confined to rare pathogenic and parasitic bacteria.
claims.source: First, by confirming the existence of Gokushovirinae prophages in free-living bacteria, we resolved a seeming paradox in which a diverse and widespread lineage within the Microviridae appeared to be confined to rare pathogenic and parasitic bacteria, such as Chlamydia (Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the discovery of enterogokushoviruses in free-living bacteria.

claims.claim: By demonstrating the integration of a gokushovirus into the E. coli genome, it was shown that these phages employ survival strategies beyond the lytic infection of hosts.
claims.source: Second, by demonstrating the integration of a gokushovirus into the E. coli genome, we show that these phages employ survival strategies beyond the lytic infection of hosts.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental demonstration of lysogeny.

claims.claim: Enterogokushoviruses appropriate a highly conserved bacterial chromosome concatemer-resolution system that enables their integration into host genomes via homologous recombination.
claims.source: Experimental characterization of the enterogokushovirus EC6098 isolated from an environmental strain of E. marmotae showed that these phages possess a dif-like recognition motif that, together with the host-encoded recombinases XerC/XerD, is required for lysogeny. In this manner, enterogokushoviruses appropriate a highly conserved bacterial chromosome concatemer-resolution system that enables their integration into host genomes via homologous recombination (Castillo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The exact mechanism of the integration process still remains to be elucidated.
claims.source: The exact mechanism of this integration process still remains to be elucidated: some phages and mobile elements are known to have different requirements for the bacterial XerC and/or XerD proteins (Midonet and Barre, 2015), which is perhaps the reason why we could only successfully reconstitute xerC but not xerD knockouts.
claims.evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study and cites relevant literature.

claims.claim: Phages with only partial DNA-binding motifs exist in a condition in which circularized phage genomes are present in the cytoplasm and virions are continuously released from the host.
claims.source: We also show that phages with only partial DNA-binding motifs exist in a condition in which circularized phage genomes are present in the cytoplasm and virions are continuously released from the host.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental results with mutant phages.

claims.claim: This strategy is similar to the pseudolysogenic state observed in crAssphage and other bacteriophages.
claims.source: While it should be noted that this could be a laboratory-induced phenomenon, this strategy is similar to the pseudolysogenic state observed in crAssphage (Shkoporov et al., 2018) and other bacteriophages (Siringan et al., 2014), and helps explain the persistence of microviruses in the human gut (Minot et al., 2013; Shkoporov et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previously described phenomena, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The sporadic distribution of dif-motifs among other gokushoviruses indicates that the ability to lysogenize bacterial hosts has been independently gained and lost multiple times during the evolution of this taxon.
claims.source: Despite an exhaustive sampling of gokushoviral diversity from metagenomic datasets, the occurrence of dif-positive gokushoviruses is rare outside of the enterogokushoviruses. However, the sporadic distribution of dif-motifs among other gokushoviruses indicates that the ability to lysogenize bacterial hosts has been independently gained and lost multiple times during the evolution of this taxon.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of dif-motifs.

claims.claim: The exclusively lytic gokushoviruses of Chlamydia might once have been able to integrate into their hosts' genomes since extant Chlamydia genomes contain coding sequences similar to the gokushoviral replication initiation and minor capsid proteins.

results.result: Bioinformatic analysis identified 95 gokushovirus prophages integrated into enterobacterial genomes, primarily in Escherichia species. These prophages are 4300-4700 bp in length with a conserved six-gene arrangement (VP4, VP5, VP3, VP1, VP2, VP8) and are flanked by dif-motifs. The prophages form distinct phylogenetic clades (A-J) with >95% nucleotide identity within clades, and show variable distribution across host phylogenies.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C44 and C112 provide comprehensive bioinformatic evidence for the discovery and characterization of enterogokushovirus prophages. The methodology (BLAST search with appropriate E-value cutoffs), genomic analysis (gene arrangement, size range, sequence variation patterns), phylogenetic analysis (bootstrap support, clade structure), and metadata analysis (host sources, O-serotypes) are well-documented and internally consistent. The data are presented in Figure 1 and supplementary files.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis of 855 gokushovirus genomes shows that enterobacterial prophages form a well-supported monophyletic clade (97% bootstrap support) within Gokushovirinae, justifying the proposed new genus 'Enterogokushovirus'. Dif-motifs are rare outside this clade, detected in only 48 of 855 genomes, highlighting the distinctiveness of enterogokushoviruses.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 demonstrate robust phylogenetic support for the proposed genus through appropriate methods (concatenated VP1/VP4 alignment, 855 genomes, bootstrap analysis). The 97% bootstrap support is strong, and the >50% average nucleotide identity within the clade supports taxonomic distinction. The comparative analysis of dif-motif distribution (48/855 genomes) provides context for the uniqueness of enterogokushoviruses. Data are shown in Figure 2.

results.result: Enterogokushoviruses are rare in metagenomic datasets and bacterial genome databases. Only 2 prophages were assembled from 1839 metagenomic samples, and fewer than 100 prophages were detected among >100,000 sequenced enterobacterial genomes, with none found in other bacterial taxa.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C95-C97 document the rarity of enterogokushoviruses through systematic searches of large datasets. The low detection rate (2/1839 metagenomes, <100/100,000+ genomes) is clearly stated and provides important ecological context. However, the claim acknowledges this is surprising given the depth of sampling, suggesting potential biological or methodological explanations discussed elsewhere in the manuscript.

results.result: Viable phage EC6098 was successfully reconstituted from a prophage sequence by PCR amplification, circularization, and transformation into E. coli DH5α. Only 1 of 4 attempted prophage reconstructions (EC6098) produced infectious particles. Electron microscopy confirmed EC6098 virions are tailless icosahedra 25-30 nm in size with a buoyant density of ~1.3 g/cm³.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59, C110-C111 describe a successful phage resurrection experiment with appropriate controls (C56) and validation (C57). The methodology is clearly described and shown in Figure 3. The electron microscopy data (C58, C110) with size measurements and buoyant density (C111) are consistent with known Microviridae properties. The low success rate (1/4) is honestly reported and corroborated by PCR detection of circular genomes in all strains but plaque formation only in EC6098.

results.result: Phage EC6098 integrates into the E. coli BW25113 genome at the dif-motif site (position 3,046,436-3,046,463) via XerC/XerD-mediated recombination. Integration requires both host recombinases (XerC and XerD) and complete phage dif-motifs, as demonstrated by knockout and complementation experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65, C113 provide strong experimental evidence for XerC/XerD-mediated integration through multiple complementary approaches: PCR detection of integration (C60-C61), sequencing confirmation of integration site (C62, C113), knockout experiments showing requirement for both XerC and XerD (C63), successful complementation of ΔxerC (C64), and phage dif-motif mutant analysis (C65). The data are shown in Figure 4 and Table 1. However, C82 acknowledges that xerD complementation failed, indicating incomplete mechanistic understanding.

results.result: Integration is reversible, with continuous excision and reintegration occurring in lysogenic cultures. Mixed populations of lysogenic and non-lysogenic cells persist in clonal colonies with a median ratio of ~4:1 lysogens to non-lysogens, indicating dynamic equilibrium.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 demonstrate reversible integration through PCR detection of both integrated and excised forms in the same colonies (C67), persistence through multiple re-streaking rounds (C68), and quantification of the lysogen ratio (C68). The inference of continuous XerC/XerD-mediated excision/reintegration (C69) is reasonable given the known properties of the XerC/XerD system and the observed mixed populations. Data are shown in Figure 4C-D.

results.result: Phages can persist cytoplasmically without integration. Bacterial colonies surviving infection contain circular phage DNA regardless of integration status, and this confers superinfection immunity. Non-integrated phages produce significantly more infectious particles than integrated prophages (p<0.01).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 demonstrate pseudolysogeny through detection of circular phage DNA in non-lysogenic survivors (C70), superinfection immunity assays (C71), quantitative comparison of phage production (C72 with statistical test), and inverse PCR ruling out alternative integration sites (C73). The inference of cytoplasmic persistence (C74) is well-supported by these observations. Data are shown in Figure 5A-B.

results.result: Serial transfer experiments over one month show that lysogenic cultures continuously produce phage, while one-third of non-lysogenic cultures (with phages present only cytoplasmically) retain phage production despite lack of integration, demonstrating stable pseudolysogeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 provide experimental evidence for long-term persistence through serial transfer experiments with appropriate controls (BW25113ΔfhuA host to avoid false positives from contaminating phages, C114). The one-month duration with 1:1000 dilutions provides strong evidence for stable maintenance. The conclusion that gokushoviruses can exist as pseudolysogens (C77) is well-supported by the combined data. Results are shown in Figure 5C.

results.result: EC6098 integrates via XerC/XerD-mediated recombination of phage-encoded dif-motifs with bacterial dif-motifs, appropriating a conserved bacterial chromosome-dimer resolution system. This capability has evolved independently in multiple gokushovirus lineages, though the exact mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C28, C81-C82 synthesize the integration mechanism findings. The XerC/XerD-mediated integration is well-demonstrated experimentally (C27, C81). The inference of independent evolution (C28) is supported by the sporadic phylogenetic distribution of dif-motifs (C48-C49). The acknowledgment that the exact mechanism is not fully understood (C82), particularly regarding differential XerC/XerD requirements, is appropriate given the failed xerD complementation.

results.result: Gokushoviruses can reliably infect and lysogenize hosts by hijacking the XerC/XerD chromosome-dimer resolution system. Sequence motifs required for lysogeny are detectable in other gokushoviruses, and even partial motifs enable cytoplasmic persistence without host culture collapse. This ability to employ multiple survival strategies likely explains their global distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 represent the main conclusions of the abstract. C3 is supported by the integration experiments (C27, C63-C65). C4 is supported by the bioinformatic detection of dif-motifs in other gokushoviruses (C48-C50). C5 is supported by the pseudolysogeny experiments (C70-C77). C6 is a reasonable inference connecting these findings to the known ecological distribution of gokushoviruses, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The discovery of Enterogokushovirus resolves the paradox of widespread gokushoviruses being known only from rare intracellular bacteria, demonstrates survival strategies beyond lytic infection, and provides new directions for studying Microviridae including a genetically manipulable model system.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80, C104-C107, C109 represent the broader significance and implications of the work. The resolution of the host range paradox (C79) is well-supported by the discovery of prophages in free-living enterobacteria. The demonstration of lysogenic and pseudolysogenic strategies (C80) is experimentally validated. The statements about future research directions (C104-C107, C109) are reasonable projections based on the findings.

results.result: Phages with partial dif-motifs exist in a pseudolysogenic state with cytoplasmic circular genomes and continuous virion release, similar to crAssphage. The sporadic distribution of dif-motifs indicates independent gain and loss of lysogenic ability during gokushovirus evolution, with evidence suggesting Chlamydia phages may have lost this capability.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 synthesize findings on pseudolysogeny and evolutionary patterns. C83 is supported by experimental data (C70-C77). The comparison to crAssphage (C84) is appropriate and supported by citations. The inference about independent evolution (C85) is supported by phylogenetic distribution (C48-C49). The speculation about Chlamydia phages (C86) is appropriately tentative and supported by genomic evidence from cited literature.

results.result: Lysogenic cultures produce fewer phage particles but are more stable than non-lysogenic cultures, representing different life history tradeoffs. The evolution of lysogeny in enterogokushoviruses is likely driven by low host abundance (<0.1% of gut microbiome), contrasting with lytic microviruses that infect abundant Bacteroidetes. High mutation rates in ssDNA phages facilitate de novo evolution of XerCD-binding motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C94 provide ecological and evolutionary context. The experimental observation of differential phage production (C87) is supported by Figure 5B. The inference about tradeoffs (C88) is reasonable. The theoretical framework about lysogeny and host scarcity (C89-C90) is well-established and appropriately cited. The connection to host abundance (C92-C93) is supported by Human Microbiome Project data. The inference about mutation-driven dif-motif evolution (C94) is reasonable given cited mutation rates, though somewhat speculative.

results.result: The rarity of gokushovirus prophages may result from dif-motif-mediated integration facilitating continuous excision and phage production. This contrasts with CTX phage which destroys its dif site to prevent excision. The environmental abundance of gokushoviruses suggests they are typically transient chromosomal residents, usually existing in pseudolysogenic or lytic states.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C103 provide mechanistic explanation for prophage rarity. The inference connecting reversible integration to prophage rarity (C98-C99) is reasonable given the experimental observations (C66-C69) and known XerC/XerD properties. The comparisons to CTX phage and other Vibrio prophages (C100-C102) are appropriately cited. The conclusion about transient chromosomal residence (C103) is a reasonable synthesis of the experimental and metagenomic data.

results.result: Background context on gokushoviruses: they are widespread in metagenomic datasets from diverse environments, easily assembled due to small circular genomes, but rarely isolated (only from three intracellular bacterial genera). They lack genes present in phiX174 including peptidoglycan synthesis inhibitors and major spike proteins, suggesting different molecular mechanisms. No gokushoviruses encode integrases, leading to the assumption they are exclusively lytic.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C24 provide literature-based background context that is well-supported by multiple citations to previous work. These claims establish the knowledge gap that the current study addresses: the paradox of widespread but rarely isolated gokushoviruses, their genomic differences from phiX174, and the assumption of exclusively lytic lifestyle. The claims are appropriately cited and provide necessary context for the study's significance.

results.result: This study detected numerous gokushovirus prophages in enterobacteria and successfully cultivated a novel gokushovirus (EC6098) capable of lysogenizing enterobacteria, representing the first isolation of a gokushovirus able to infect free-living bacteria and integrate as a lysogen.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26, C30, C59 summarize the main achievements of the study. The detection of prophages (C25) is supported by bioinformatic analysis (C31-C44). The cultivation of EC6098 (C26) is supported by experimental data (C54-C58). The claim of novelty (C59) is justified given previous gokushoviruses were only isolated from intracellular bacteria (C16) and were thought to be exclusively lytic (C19). This represents a major advance in the field.

results.result: An intermediate pseudolysogenic state exists between lytic and lysogenic lifestyles in gokushoviruses, where phages persist cytoplasmically without integration while continuously producing virions.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 represents a key finding supported by multiple lines of evidence: detection of circular phage DNA in non-lysogenic survivors (C70), superinfection immunity without integration (C71), higher phage production in non-lysogenic cultures (C72), and long-term persistence in serial transfers (C76). The characterization as an 'intermediate' state between lytic and lysogenic is appropriate given the continuous phage production (unlike true lysogeny) but stable host-phage coexistence (unlike acute lytic infection).

results.result: The Alpavirinae have been detected as prophages of Bacteroidetes but remain without isolates and lack official recognition, representing a promising target for future isolation efforts using similar resurrection approaches.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is a minor point about future research directions, appropriately cited to previous work (Roux et al., 2012). It suggests the methodology developed in this study could be applied to other Microviridae subfamilies. This is a reasonable suggestion but represents future work rather than a result of the current study.
